transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
In the tech world, chip giant Nvidia
has reinstated Jensen Wong as CEO.
Wall Street rallied and MegaSpeed.
The company associated with a suspected Chinese spy
entangled with Wong is now on a commerce department
blacklist, NPR Shannon Bond reports.
The commerce department is adding MegaSpeed
to a list of companies barred from buying advanced technology
without a US government license.
The justice department has said
it's conducting a criminal investigation
into allegations MegaSpeed has enabled China
to illegally access Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Wong, resigned earlier this month
after reports he had an affair with a MegaSpeed executive
who US officials suspect was working
with Chinese intelligence.
This week, Nvidia's board reversed course
and reinstated Wong.
MegaSpeed didn't respond to a request for comment.
It previously denied wrongdoing
and said the executive left the company last year.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
- A federal appeals court has cleared the way
for the army to detonate lead-based explosives
at an Iowa facility.
The army says the detonation will happen Wednesday morning,
but several issues remain unclear.
Iowa Public Radio's Grant Gerlach reports.
- President Donald Trump said the detonation was on pause
until the Eighth Circuit ruled in favor of the operation.
Now the court says it can go forward.
The controlled explosion of nearly five tons
of lead azide at the Iowa Army ammunition plant
has raised alarm because it will create
a drifting cloud of lead dust.
The judge's ruling says the EPA has taken necessary steps
to minimize the spread.
Preparations include sand barriers
stacked two stories high around the stored explosives.
Trump also says incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand
must approve the operation.
Sand says the administration should decide based
on information from experts on the ground.
For NPR News, I'm Grant Gerlach.
- Storms on both coasts could sully the Thanksgiving holiday.
For those hoping to enjoy the 100th,
Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade,
a big storm brewing along the East Coast
could ground those big balloons we all know and love.
Along the Pacific Coast,
specifically in the San Francisco Bay Area,
tides are expected to reach 2.8 feet above normal by tomorrow.
The National Weather Service warns these king tides,
amplified by a super El Nino,
could be the highest in over four decades.
A high surf warning is in effect
with waves reaching up to 30 feet.
And Washington State ferries are already canceling sailings
due to high tides.
One of the biggest Thanksgiving costs every year
is not the turkey or the cranberry sauce.
It's the travel, NPR's Joe Hernandez.
- AAA said in its Thanksgiving forecast
that it expects near record levels of travel this year,
81.5 million people are expected to travel
at least 50 miles from home.
That's actually a bit lower than last year,
partly because of high fuel costs.
- You're listening to NPR.
New research shows people taking GLP-1 drugs for weight loss
may also see higher breast density in subsequent mammograms.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi reports.
- The study being presented
at the Radiological Society of America
looked back at 107 women, age 39 to 79,
who had gotten mammograms before and after
starting a regimen of GLP-1 drugs like Wagovie or ZEP found.
Breast density increased for 62.5% of women.
Normally, dense breasts are associated
with higher breast cancer risk,
in part because the fibroglangellar tissue
can obscure tumors.
But in this case, researchers are not yet certain
that the tissue composition of the breast
or the cancer risk changes with GLP-1 use.
The researchers advise people taking the drugs
to continue routine breast cancer screening as recommended.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
- It is time for the annual White House Turkey Pardon.
President Trump will follow the longstanding tradition
of pardoning two turkeys.
This year's Lucky Birds, who will not end up
on the dinner table, are named Freedom and Feathers.
While both will be pardoned,
only one will get the ceremonial treatment during
today's White House event.
Which one will it be?
The public can vote online to decide on the in-person honor.
Both turkeys will live out their days
at Texas A&M University,
where they will be cared for and pampered.
This will be the 79th Turkey Pardoning,
although the tradition did not become an annual event
until George H.W. Bush's administration.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News.

topics.text: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after suspected Chinese spy affair; MegaSpeed blacklisted
Federal appeals court clears army to detonate lead azide explosives at Iowa ammunition plant
Storms and king tides threaten Macy's Thanksgiving Parade and Pacific Coast, high surf warnings issued
AAA forecasts 81.5 million Thanksgiving travelers, slightly lower than last year due to fuel costs
Study finds GLP-1 weight-loss drug users show higher breast density in subsequent mammograms
Trump to pardon Thanksgiving turkeys Freedom and Feathers; public votes on ceremonial bird
